spot.title: Distance modulus: which way does the sign go?
spot.intro: A star has apparent magnitude $m=12.0$ and absolute magnitude $M=2.0$. Find its distance. One step of the solution below is wrong.
steps: So the star is closer than any known star, and it would appear very bright.
spot.why: Inverting $m-M=5\log_{10}(d/10\,\mathrm{pc})$ gives a positive exponent. The star is fainter than its absolute magnitude (m > M), so it must be farther than 10 pc, not nearer.

source.where: adapted from Open Q1 (SN Ia magnitude), topic distance modulus

spot.title: Wien peak to luminosity of a hot star
spot.intro: A star radiates as a blackbody with peak wavelength $\lambda_\mathrm{max}=290\,\mathrm{nm}$ and radius $R=2\,R_\odot$. Find $L/L_\odot$ with $L_\odot=3.83\times10^{26}\,\mathrm{W}$. One step is wrong.
steps: Emitting area: the star's disc, $A=\pi R^2 = 6.07\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{m^2}$.
spot.why: The star emits from its whole spherical surface, not only from the projected disc. Using $\pi R^2$ instead of $4\pi R^2$ loses a factor 4.

source.where: adapted from Open Q3 (MS star, Wien peak, T_eff), topic Stefan-Boltzmann

spot.title: From extinction in magnitudes to optical depth
spot.intro: Dust dims a background star by $A_V = 2.0$ mag. Find the optical depth $\tau$ along the line of sight. One step is wrong.
steps: Pure absorption in the slab: $F = F_0\,e^{-\tau}$.
Since $\tau<1$ the dust screen is optically thin.
spot.why: The exponential $e^{-\tau}$ has to be inverted with the natural logarithm, not $\log_{10}$. Mixing the two logs is the classic slip: $A_V = 1.086\,\tau$, not $A_V=\tau$.
spot.fix: $\tau = -\ln(0.158) = 1.84$ (equivalently $A_V/1.086$). The screen is optically thick at $\tau>1$.

source.where: adapted from Open Q4 (extinction vs Galactic latitude), topic optical depth and magnitudes

spot.title: Eddington luminosity of a supermassive black hole
spot.intro: Compute $L_\mathrm{Edd}$ for a black hole of $10^{7}\,M_\odot$ using the balance of radiation force on electrons and gravity. One step is wrong.
steps: Radiation force per electron at radius $r$: $F_\mathrm{rad}=\sigma_T L/(4\pi r^2 c)$.
Electrons are coupled to protons by the Coulomb force, so gravity acts on the pair: $F_\mathrm{grav}= GM m_p/r^2$.
Setting $F_\mathrm{rad}=F_\mathrm{grav}$, the factor $r^2$ cancels: $L_\mathrm{Edd}=4\pi G M m_p c/\sigma_T$.
Insert numbers with the electron mass, since electrons feel the radiation: $m=m_e=9.1\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
spot.why: The radiation acts on electrons but the inertia/gravity is carried by the protons they are bound to, so $m_p$ appears. Using $m_e$ underestimates $L_\mathrm{Edd}$ by $m_p/m_e\approx1836$, in contradiction with step 2.
spot.fix: $L_\mathrm{Edd}=4\pi G M m_p c/\sigma_T \approx 1.26\times10^{31}\,\mathrm{W}\,(M/M_\odot)=1.26\times10^{38}\,\mathrm{W}$ for $10^7 M_\odot$.

source.where: adapted from Open Q3 (hydrostatic equilibrium to Eddington luminosity), topic Eddington limit

spot.title: Virial mass of a galaxy cluster
spot.intro: Galaxies in a cluster of radius $R=1\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ have a line-of-sight velocity dispersion $\sigma=1000\,\mathrm{km/s}$. Estimate the mass. One step is wrong.
steps: Measured: $\sigma$ is the dispersion of one velocity component only.
Virial theorem: $2K+U=0$ with $K=\tfrac12 M\langle v^2\rangle$ and $U\approx -GM^2/R$.
So $M\langle v^2\rangle = GM^2/R$, i.e. $M = R\langle v^2\rangle/G$.
spot.why: The 3D mean square speed is the sum of three components: $\langle v^2\rangle = 3\sigma^2$ for isotropic orbits. The line-of-sight dispersion is only one of them.

source.where: adapted from Open Q5 (cluster L_X via virial) and Q5 of the practice exam, topic virial theorem

spot.title: How the Jeans mass changes in an isothermal collapse
spot.intro: A cloud collapses isothermally and its density rises by a factor 100. How does the Jeans mass change? One step is wrong.
steps: Isothermal means $T$ is constant, and $\rho$ grows by 100.
Therefore $M_J\propto\rho^{-3/2}$ drops by a factor $100^{3/2}=1000$, so small fragments become unstable.
spot.why: At fixed $T$, step 3 gives $M_J\propto\rho^{-1/2}$. The exponent $-3/2$ is that of $\lambda_J^3$ alone; it ignores the factor $\rho$ in $M_J\sim\rho\lambda_J^3$.
spot.fix: $M_J\propto\rho^{-1/2}$ falls by $100^{1/2}=10$; fragmentation still follows, only less dramatically.

source.where: adapted from Ch. 8.3, topic Jeans instability

spot.title: Age of a flat matter-dominated universe: units trap
spot.intro: Estimate the age of a flat, matter-only universe with $H_0=70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$. One step is wrong.
spot.why: The kilometre was not converted to metres. $70\,\mathrm{km}=7\times10^4\,\mathrm{m}$, so the numerator must be $7\times10^4$. The result 9 Tyr is absurd (older than any star) and should trigger a sanity check.

source.where: adapted from Open Q7 (Friedmann, a(t)), topic matter-dominated age

spot.title: Hubble-law distance from a measured redshift
spot.intro: The H$\alpha$ line (656.3 nm) of a galaxy is observed at 722 nm. Use $H_0=70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$. One step is wrong.
steps: So $z=0.100$, small enough for the low-redshift approximation.
This is far beyond the observable universe, which is odd for $z=0.1$.
spot.why: The Hubble law is $v=H_0 d$, so $d=v/H_0$. Multiplying gives units of $\mathrm{km^2\,s^{-2}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, not Mpc, and an impossible distance.

source.where: adapted from Ch. 10.3-10.4, topic Hubble law and redshift

spot.title: Main-sequence lifetime of a 10 solar-mass star
spot.intro: Using $L\propto M^3$ and a Sun lifetime $t_\odot=10\,\mathrm{Gyr}$, estimate the main-sequence lifetime of a $10\,M_\odot$ star. One step is wrong.
steps: Fuel available is proportional to the mass: $E\propto M$.
Lifetime is fuel over burning rate: $t = E/L \propto M/L$.
$t = 1000\,\mathrm{Gyr}$: massive stars live far longer than the Sun.
spot.why: Step 3 says $t\propto M/L$, but step 4 inserts $L/M$, inverting the ratio. A bright star burns out faster; a result of 1000 Gyr (far above the age of the universe) is a red flag.

source.where: adapted from Open Q3 (10 Msun star), topic M-L scaling and MS lifetime

spot.title: Flat rotation curve from an isothermal halo
spot.intro: A halo has density $\rho(r)=\rho_0 r_0^2/r^2$. Show that the circular speed is independent of $r$. One step is wrong.
steps: This does not depend on $r$, so the rotation curve is flat.
spot.why: The mass element is $dM=4\pi r'^2\rho\,dr'$. The factor $4\pi$ from the solid angle was dropped, which rescales the plateau speed by $\sqrt{4\pi}$ even though the flatness conclusion survives.

source.where: adapted from Open Q6 (flat rotation curve, escape velocity), topic isothermal halo

spot.title: Temperature during the radiation era
spot.intro: At $t=1\,\mathrm{s}$ the temperature is $10^{10}\,\mathrm{K}$. Estimate $T$ at $t=100\,\mathrm{s}$ in the radiation era. One step is wrong.
spot.why: $a\propto t^{2/3}$ holds for matter. With $H^2\propto a^{-4}$, $\dot a\,a=\mathrm{const}$ so $a\propto t^{1/2}$ in the radiation era.

source.where: adapted from Open Q7 (radiation era, T(a), BBN), topic a(t) in radiation era

limits.title: Adding mass to a white dwarf
limits.prompt: In the non-relativistic degenerate limit ($P\propto\rho^{5/3}$) a white dwarf gains mass. What happens to its radius?
options: It grows, like for a normal star
It stays constant
It shrinks, $R\propto M^{-1/3}$
It shrinks until it reaches the Schwarzschild radius
limits.explain: Balancing $P\sim GM^2/R^4$ with $P\propto\rho^{5/3}\propto (M/R^3)^{5/3}$ gives $R\propto M^{-1/3}$. More massive white dwarfs are smaller; the relativistic correction then stops the trend near $M_\mathrm{Ch}$.

source.where: Ch. 5.2-5.3 (white dwarfs, Chandrasekhar), topic degeneracy limits

limits.title: Ultra-relativistic degeneracy
limits.prompt: In the ultra-relativistic degenerate limit $P\propto\rho^{4/3}$. What does hydrostatic equilibrium then require?
options: Any mass is stable with a suitable radius
A unique mass, independent of radius (the Chandrasekhar mass)
The radius to go to infinity as $M$ grows
The star to be stable only for $M\to0$
limits.explain: With $P\sim K\rho^{4/3}$ both the pressure and the gravitational requirement scale as $M^{2/3}/R^4$ versus $M^2/R^4$: the radius cancels and only one mass, $M_\mathrm{Ch}\approx1.4\,M_\odot$, satisfies equilibrium. Above it the star collapses.

source.where: Ch. 5.3 (Chandrasekhar limit)

limits.title: What dominates the early universe?
limits.prompt: In the Friedmann equation with matter ($\propto a^{-3}$), radiation ($\propto a^{-4}$), curvature ($\propto a^{-2}$) and $\Lambda$ ($\propto a^0$), which term dominates as $a\to0$?
options: Matter
Curvature
Radiation
The cosmological constant
limits.explain: At small $a$ the steepest power of $1/a$ wins: radiation. Curvature and $\Lambda$ matter only later, which is why the early universe looks flat and $a\propto t^{1/2}$ at first.

source.where: Open Q7 (radiation era) and MC on Friedmann terms

limits.title: Late-time fate with a cosmological constant
limits.prompt: If $\Omega_\Lambda>0$ and the universe keeps expanding, what happens to $a(t)$ at very late times?
options: $a\propto t^{2/3}$ forever
$a\propto t^{1/2}$
$a\propto e^{Ht}$ with $H=\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$ constant
$a$ reaches a maximum and recollapses
limits.explain: Matter and curvature terms fall as $a^{-3}$, $a^{-2}$ while the $\Lambda$ term is constant, so eventually $H^2\to\Lambda/3$ and the expansion is exponential (de Sitter). Recollapse needs positive curvature dominating, not $\Lambda>0$.

source.where: Open Q7 (Friedmann, a(t))

limits.title: Curvature and the closed universe
limits.prompt: In a closed universe ($k=+1$) without $\Lambda$, the Friedmann equation $\dot a^2=\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho a^2-kc^2$ implies what for the expansion?
options: It continues forever with $\dot a\to c$
It stops at a maximum $a_\mathrm{max}$ where $\dot a=0$, then recollapses
It stops at a finite $a$ and stays static
It accelerates
limits.explain: As $\rho a^2\propto a^{-1}$ (matter) decreases, the first term eventually falls below $kc^2$, so $\dot a^2=0$ at $a_\mathrm{max}$ and the universe recollapses, giving a finite lifetime.

source.where: Open Q7 (closed universe, lifetime)

limits.title: High vs low mass: main-sequence lifetime
limits.prompt: Compared to the Sun, a $20\,M_\odot$ main-sequence star has a lifetime that is:
options: Longer, since it has more fuel
About the same, since fuel and luminosity both scale with $M$
Much shorter, since $L$ grows faster than $M$
Shorter only because it is hotter, not because of $L$
limits.explain: $t\propto M/L$ and $L\propto M^{3}$ or steeper, so $t\propto M^{-2}$ or steeper: tens of Myr instead of 10 Gyr. This sets why massive stars are rare relics of recent star formation.

source.where: Open Q3 (10 Msun star), MC on lifetimes

limits.title: pp chain vs CNO cycle
limits.prompt: Why does the CNO cycle dominate energy generation in stars somewhat more massive than the Sun?
options: It needs less temperature than the pp chain
Its rate rises much more steeply with temperature ($\epsilon\propto T^{\sim16}$ versus $T^{\sim4}$) and massive stars have hotter cores
More massive stars have no hydrogen to fuse in pp
CNO is not affected by the Coulomb barrier
limits.explain: Both cycles must overcome the Coulomb barrier, but CNO involves higher charge, so its rate is far more sensitive to $T$. Above a core temperature of roughly $1.7\times10^7\,\mathrm{K}$ it wins, and it drives convective cores.

source.where: Ch. 4.1-4.3 (pp chain, CNO cycle)

limits.title: Hot gas versus the virial temperature
limits.prompt: A cluster potential well has a virial temperature $kT_\mathrm{vir}\sim G M\mu m_p/R$. Gas at $T\gg T_\mathrm{vir}$ will:
options: Collapse rapidly into the centre
Stay in hydrostatic equilibrium by exact balance
Have pressure exceeding gravitational binding and flow out (or be heated further from the outside)
Cool by Compton scattering to $T_\mathrm{vir}$ at once
limits.explain: Gas can stay bound only if its thermal energy per particle is of order the potential depth. At $T\gg T_\mathrm{vir}$ it is energetically unbound, while at $T\ll T_\mathrm{vir}$ it falls inwards until pressure support builds up. This is the basis of the L_X estimate via the virial theorem.

source.where: Open Q5 (thermal bremsstrahlung cluster via virial)

limits.title: Jeans length: small and large scales
limits.prompt: A perturbation in a gas cloud has a wavelength $\lambda$. What distinguishes $\lambda\ll\lambda_J$ from $\lambda\gg\lambda_J$?
options: Both collapse, only on different timescales
$\lambda\ll\lambda_J$ oscillates as a sound wave; $\lambda\gg\lambda_J$ grows (collapses) because gravity beats pressure
$\lambda\ll\lambda_J$ collapses; $\lambda\gg\lambda_J$ oscillates
Neither changes because the cloud is in equilibrium
limits.explain: The sound-crossing time over a scale $\lambda$ is $\lambda/c_s$. If it is shorter than the free-fall time pressure can respond and the mode oscillates; if longer, gravity wins. The boundary is $\lambda_J\sim c_s/\sqrt{G\rho}$.

source.where: Ch. 8.3 (Jeans instability)

limits.title: Black-hole growth at the Eddington limit
limits.prompt: A black hole accretes at its Eddington luminosity with radiative efficiency $\eta$. How does its mass grow?
options: Linearly, $M\propto t$
Exponentially, with an e-folding (Salpeter) time independent of $M$
It cannot grow since radiation pressure stops the infall
limits.explain: $L_\mathrm{Edd}\propto M$ and $\dot M=(1-\eta)L/(\eta c^2)\propto M$, so $M\propto e^{t/t_S}$ with $t_S=\frac{\eta}{1-\eta}\frac{\sigma_T c}{4\pi G m_p}\approx 50\,\mathrm{Myr}$ for $\eta=0.1$, independent of $M$. It sets the timescale for forming quasars at high $z$.

source.where: Open Q6 (BH accretion growth, Eddington time)

limits.title: Collisional or collisionless?
limits.prompt: A galaxy has $N\sim10^{11}$ stars. Compared with the Hubble time, its two-body relaxation time $t_\mathrm{relax}\approx\frac{N}{8\ln N}t_\mathrm{cross}$ is:
options: Much shorter, so stars exchange energy often
Comparable to the age of the Universe
Much longer, so the stars move in the smooth mean potential (collisionless)
Independent of $N$
limits.explain: With $t_\mathrm{cross}\sim10^8$ yr, $t_\mathrm{relax}\sim10^{8}\cdot10^{11}/(8\cdot25)\sim5\times10^{16}$ yr, far above the Hubble time. Galaxies are collisionless; globular clusters with $N\sim10^5$ are not.

source.where: Open Q4 (galaxy with BH and halo) and Ch. 7.2 on relaxation

limits.title: Rotation curve regimes
limits.prompt: For a galaxy with a central black hole of mass $M_\mathrm{BH}$ and an $r^{-2}$ halo, how does $v_c(r)$ behave at small and at large $r$?
options: $v_c\propto r$ at small $r$ and $\propto r^{-1/2}$ at large $r$
$v_c\propto r^{-1/2}$ (Keplerian) at small $r$ and constant at large $r$
$v_c$ is constant everywhere
$v_c\propto r^{-1/2}$ at both ends
limits.explain: From $v_c^2=GM_\mathrm{BH}/r+4\pi G\rho_0r_0^2$: the point mass dominates when $r$ is small ($v\propto r^{-1/2}$), the halo term gives a flat $v_c$ far out.

source.where: Open Q4 (galaxy with BH and r^-2 halo)

limits.title: Stroemgren radius and density
limits.prompt: An HII region around an O star with ionizing photon rate $Q$ lies in uniform gas of density $n$. If $n$ doubles at fixed $Q$, the Stroemgren radius:
options: Doubles
Halves
Decreases by $2^{-2/3}\approx0.63$
Is unchanged since $Q$ is fixed
limits.explain: Ionization balance: $Q=\frac43\pi R_S^3\,n^2\alpha_B$, so $R_S\propto (Q/n^2)^{1/3}\propto n^{-2/3}$. Denser gas recombines faster, so the same photon budget ionizes a smaller volume.

source.where: Open Q4 (HII region, ionizing photon balance)

limits.title: Distances at low and high redshift
limits.prompt: Which statement about cosmological distances is correct?
options: For $z\ll1$ all distance measures agree with $cz/H_0$; at high $z$ they differ and $d_L=(1+z)^2d_A$
$d_L=d_A$ at all redshifts
$d_L$ is always smaller than $d_A$ at low $z$
$d_L=cz/H_0$ exactly at every $z$
limits.explain: At $z\ll1$ every definition reduces to $d\approx cz/H_0$. Beyond that they depend on the expansion history, and the Etherington relation $d_L=(1+z)^2d_A$ always holds for flux versus angular size.

source.where: Ch. 10.3-10.4 (redshift, distances)
